amendments.rule: The article `הַ` aligns to English *the*. Hebrew has no indefinite article, so an English *a* or *an* belongs to the noun that licenses it and is not `added`. **The same ownership applies to a definite article the ASV supplies where no Hebrew article morpheme is present:** it belongs to the nominal expression it determines and is not `added`. **Read that as the noun of the expression, not as its leftmost word.** Where the expression writes both a numeral and the noun it counts, the supplied determiner joins that noun's unit and the numeral takes only its own word: `בַּחֲמִשָּׁה עָשָׂר יוֹם` → *the fifteenth day* gives *the day* to `יוֹם` and *fifteenth* to the numeral, and `לִשְׁלֹשָׁה עָשָׂר פָּרִים` → *of the thirteen bullocks* and `לְאַרְבָּעָה עָשָׂר כְּבָשִׂים` → *of the fourteen lambs* give *the bullocks* and *the lambs* to their nouns. A numeral takes such a determiner only where the Hebrew writes no noun for it to determine, which is rule 31's substantival numeral — `בְּאֶחָד לַחֹדֶשׁ` → *on* ***the first day*** *of the month*. And this reaches a supplied determiner only: where an article morpheme stands in the phrase it takes the written *the* first, under rules 29 and 47, and where the ASV writes a distributive *each* or *every* the numeral takes that word under rule 41. **And it applies to a supplied quantifying determiner such as *any*, which is the word English writes in that same slot where *a* will not stand — under a negation, in a question, or after a comparative.** Where a bare noun carries no determiner morpheme of its own and the ASV writes an *any* before it, that word determines the nominal expression exactly as a supplied *a* or *the* does: it joins the noun's unit, is not `added`, and is never the head, which stays on the word carrying the lexeme under rule 31 — `לִמְלָאכָה` → *for any work* gives *for* to the preposition and *any work* to the noun, headed on *work*. **But only where no morpheme in the clause licenses that determiner.** A `כֹּל` standing on the noun is itself what the *any* renders and takes it, the noun keeping only its own word — `כָּל־עֵץ` → *any tree*, `כָּל־כְּלִי` → *any vessel* — and where the ASV recasts a clause's negation onto a nominal standing in it, the negative takes the determiner that negation has become. **Read which nominal the ASV has put the determiner on rather than what its grammatical role is**: an object takes it in `לֹא יֵעָשֶׂה לִמְלָאכָה` → *it was meet for* ***no*** *work*, which gives *no* to `לֹא`, discontinuous from the verb it negates under rule 25, and leaves `מְלָאכָה` the bare *work*; a subject takes it in `אַל־תָּבֹא רְנָנָה בוֹ` → *Let* ***no*** *joyful voice come therein*, which gives *no* to `אַל` and leaves the noun its own *joyful voice*. A jussive or prohibitive `אַל` is read on the same terms as `לֹא`. Count the determiners and read which morpheme each answers to, as rule 41 counts a phrase's determiners and rule 29 counts its *the*s. This does not reach a supplied possessive, which rule 18 leaves `added` where no suffix or other possessive morpheme is present. **A supplied determiner that distinguishes one member of a class from another is read on exactly those terms.** Where the ASV writes a correlative *one … another*, or another contrastive determiner standing where an *a* or a *the* would stand, before a noun that carries no determiner morpheme of its own, that word determines the nominal expression as a supplied *a* or *any* does: it joins the noun's unit, is not `added`, and is never the head. `מִמַּטֶּה לְמַטֶּה אַחֵר` → *from* ***one*** *tribe to another tribe* gives *one tribe* to the first `מַטֶּה`, headed on *tribe*, while `אַחֵר` keeps the *another* written for it. Do not read such a word as evidence that a numeral stands in the phrase, and do not mark it `added` under rule 30 because it is not one of the determiners named above: what decides it is that no morpheme in the phrase licenses the word, which is the count the preceding sentences run. But run that count first, since a numeral standing in the phrase is itself what such a word renders and takes it under rule 31 — `לְאֶחָד מִמִּשְׁפַּחַת` → *unto* ***one*** *of the family* — and one chapter may write both shapes, as NUM.36.8 and NUM.36.9 do. **For Aramaic, a separately segmented determined-state ending (`Td`) is treated likewise:** align it to *the* when the ASV writes a corresponding article, and mark it `unrepresented` under rule 29 when the ASV writes no separate article, including where another determiner supplies the determination. **A determiner that directly realizes another morpheme is not a corresponding article.** In the temporal relative `עִדָּנָא דִּי` → *what time*, *what* realizes the written relative `דִּי`, while the determined-state ending is `unrepresented`; the relative morpheme takes the word before the nominal determination does, exactly as a present `כֹּל` or negative takes its determiner above. More specific construct and substantival rules still decide which source unit inside that expression takes it.
amendments.why: NUM.36.9 renders `מִמַּטֶּה לְמַטֶּה אַחֵר` as *from one tribe to another tribe* with no numeral or determiner morpheme anywhere in the phrase, while NUM.36.8 writes a real `אֶחָד` rendered *one* two verses earlier. Rule 15 as it stood gave a supplied *a*, *an*, *the* and *any* to the noun, and defined the *any* case as the slot where *a* will not stand — which a contrastive *one* is not — so the rule did not clearly reach the word, and rule 41's sentence that a present `אֶחָד` takes a distributive determiner invites the inference that a supplied one must be `added` or must be hunting for a numeral. The amendment adds the case where the rule's own count already decides it, keeps the count itself as the test, and names the two verses that distinguish a written numeral from a supplied determiner. Nothing in the corpus tables supplied contradicts it: `מַטֶּה` is aligned to a bare *one* only where the Hebrew writes no other word for it (NUM.17.2), and no unit in the precedent marks a determiner of this kind `added` beside a noun that holds its own English.

conventions: The copular marriage formula הָיָה (+ subject) … לְנָשִׁים / לְאִשָּׁה → *be married*, *were married*, *shall be wife* is divided the same way throughout: הָיָה takes the copula together with whatever subject pronoun, modal or jussive frame the ASV writes (*they be*, *Let them be*, *shall they be*, *were*, *They were*, *shall be*), נָשִׁים or אִשָּׁה takes the lexical *married* or *wife*, and the לְ is its own unrepresented unit under rules 21 and 40, the recasting leaving nothing for its relation. Verses 3, 6 (twice), 8, 11 and 12. BSB represents that לְ; the difference is convention, not error.

אִישׁ rendered by a distributive English phrase heads on the nominal word and not on *every*: *every one* heads on *one* in vv. 7 and 9 and *every man* heads on *man* in v.8, since *every* is the distributive the phrase adds and the other word is what stands for the noun (rules 24, 31). The competing reading heads all three on *every*; it was declined so that the three units head alike whichever English noun the ASV chose. A written כֹּל is a different case and takes the *every* itself, as in v.8's כָל־בַּת.

The ASV italic *houses* in *the fathers houses* (v.1, both occurrences) is aligned into its own אָבוֹת unit as the generic supplied to complete that substantive's sense under rule 31, headed on *fathers*, rather than marked added on the strength of the italic (rule 7). The competing reading treats it as a supplied head noun under rule 20's supplied-lexical boundary and marks it added; it was declined because the phrase renders one Hebrew substantive and no event is predicated by the supplied word. Both occurrences are read the same way, and the chapter's one added unit is the italic *other* of v.3, where no morpheme stands for the word at all.

report: Checked all 26 cross-verse candidate groups. Every difference is the ASV rendering one morpheme differently in different contexts; none is one construction analysed two ways with nothing in the source to license it. No patches.

The recurring construction most at risk of a split is the copular marriage formula: הָיָה … לְנָשִׁים in NUM.36.3, 6 (twice), 11 and 12. All five are divided identically — the copula and any auxiliary or jussive frame on הָיָה, the lexical *married* on נָשִׁים, the לְ unrepresented under rules 21 and 40. NUM.36.8's לְאִשָּׁה → *shall be wife* is the same division with the predicate noun's own word written.

NUM.36.3 *And if* versus NUM.36.4 *And when* is licensed by the source rather than a split: v.4 writes אִם beside the waw, so each morpheme takes the word written for it, while v.3 writes only a waw and the contiguous coordinator-plus-subordinator pair is its single rendering under rule 55. אֲשֶׁר לָהֶם → *whereunto* is fused identically in vv. 3 and 4, headed on the relative.

עַל־פִּי is split in v.5 (*according to* on עַל, *the word* on פֶּה) while בְּיַד (v.13) and both לִפְנֵי (v.1) are fused — rule 30's one-rendering condition applied consistently, the construct noun holding an English word of its own only in v.5. אִישׁ heads on the nominal word in all three of its units (*one*, *one*, *man*), never on the distributive *every*, and כֹּל takes the *every* of v.8 because a כֹּל morpheme stands there.

BSB: the six disagreements are all לְ marked unrepresented — the lēʾmōr lamed of vv. 5 and 6 (rule 27) and the lamed of lənāšîm / ləʾiššāh in vv. 6, 8, 11 and 12 (rules 21, 40). These are the documented convention difference, BSB attaching the preposition to its phrase. None is a genuine error and none is worth changing.

The chapter's single added unit (the italic *other* of v.3) is correct, and no supplied English word is folded into a licensing morpheme in one verse and marked added in another: the supplied determiners (*any* tribe v.8, *one* tribe v.9, the supplied *the*s of rule 29) all join their nouns, and the two italic *houses* tokens both join אָבוֹת under rule 31 with the competing reading named in the unit note.

Three conventions recorded: the marriage-formula division, the head of the distributive אִישׁ phrase, and the italic *houses* judgment. One amendment to rule 15, adding the supplied contrastive *one* of *one tribe … another tribe* (v.9), which the rule's *a*/*the*/*any* sentences do not reach and which v.8's written אֶחָד makes easy to misplace.
